description.narrative: MISSION OF PROGRAMME: To strengthen the capacity and legitimacy of civil society organisations and support activities that ensure the participatory nature of political and social processes and the accountability of duty bearers. Civil society organisations will mobilise citizens and increase popular participation in decision-making, improve transparency and accountability and ensure respect for socio- economic/labour rights. OBJECTIVE 1: The programme intends to see citizens and citizen groups be empowered, organised and actively involved in organisations/networks, participating and influencing decision making processes. OBJECTIVE 2: The programme intends to see civil society organizations promote regulations related to transparency and duty-bearers to adopt and implement anti-corruption measures. OBJECTIVE 3: The programme intends to strengthen the legitimacy and capacity of trade unions and other CSOs working for increased access to decent work and the rights of workers based on core international labour conventions.

Organisation Olof Palmes Internationella Center (OPIC) har till Sida ansökt om finansiering av 34 miljoner kronor för att utföra programmet för Serbien 2016-2021. Projektet är en förtsättning på tidigare stöd med fokus på ökat åtnjutande av mänskliga rättigheter och stärkta möljigheter att utöva demokratiskt inflytande. OPIC har en unik kompetens och lång praktisk erfarenhet av demokratiutveckling och fattigdomsbekämpning och det ger OPIC goda möjligheter att arbeta för målet för svenskt utvecklingssamarbete - att bidra till att skapa förutsättningar för fattiga människor att förbättra sina levnadsvillkor.
OPICs förslag ligger i linje med den svenska resultatstrategin för reformsarbete med Öseuropa, Västra Balkan och Turkiet för perioden 2014-2020 som anger stöd till stärkt demokrati, ökad respekt för mänskliga rättigheter och mer utvecklad rättsstat. Projektet är mycket relevant för Serbiens EU integrationsagenda eftersom ett aktivt civilsamhälle kan spela en viktig roll i genomförandet och uppföljningen av nationella och EU-prioriteringar och strategier.

new OPIC Serbia 2016-2021: Over the past four years, Serbia did not make significant improvements when it comes to reform processes and European Integrations. The existing focus on transparency and accountability, citizen participation and the legitimacy of civil society organisations will therefore remain, further emphasizing the importance of activism, movement building and membership.

Overall, the programme 2016-2022 worked to build capacities of civil society organisations to become agents of change in their context. OPC supported trade unions and other organisations working with labour market related issues to promote workers rights as a necessary component for a sustainable and inclusive economic development. OPC also collaborated with civil society organisations focusing on good governance, the rule of law, transparency and gender equality, and supporting initiatives aimed at improving public service delivery, enhancing the capacity of local government institutions and promoting transparency and accountability of duty-bearers.
The programme had enchanced focus at socio-economic rights due to the existing conditions and economic trends in society. Serbia's incomplete transition has its effects on labour markets. While unemployment has further dropped (9 per cent for age of 15 and above, 2022), Serbia continues to struggle with relatively low labour force participation and high inactivity including a large portion of youth neither in employment nor in education or training. Informality continues to be high, the quality of jobs requires substantive improvement, and there is a need for further reforms of the occupational safety and health system. The long-standing labour legislation reform is relevant both for EU accession and for the advancement of social dialogue. However, the governments new economic approach was based on attraction of foreign investments through subsidies, cheap labour accompanied by weak protection of labour rights. Changes of the Labour Law in 2014 decreased the existing level of labour rights and were adopted despite strong objections by the trade unions, expert community and civil society. Government pandering to investors, inadequate labour legislation and a slow-moving judiciary are some of the reasons for widespread violations of workplace rights in Serbia.
The social power of trade unions in Serbia is generally small. Many unions are seen as undemocratic structures and while there is an urgent need for internal reforms to promote modern and constructive unions, there is also a need for connecting civil society organisations that are working on socio-economic rights and other issues related to working conditions with both the existing union structures and with new actors in this field.
The OPC under this programme continued to support an average of fifteen projects per year but the coordination between the partner organisations was on a much higher level than in the previous years. The synergetic effect was achieved through the identification of compatible projects and organisations and continuous exchange of information, expertise and joint actions. For the first time in modern history of Serbia, trade union confederations signed memorandum of cooperation with civil society organisations to use each others strengths and comparative advantages in the joint struggle for the improvement of labour rights.
Also the organisations working on transparency and accountability increasingly coordinated their work realising that individually they are an easier target for already unscrupulous continuous attacks coming from those in decision-making positions.
The total of 29 organisations were supported through the budget line External contribution with individual projects and the annual number of projects was between 15 and 18. Most of the partnerships lasted for at least three years.
Some examples of results:
The OPC worked under the programme to strengthen the dialog through joint activities of all actors involved in labour rights including trade unions and local organisations dealing with marginalized groups. The programme implementing partner Uzice Center for Human Rights and Democracy (UCHRD) was focused at this work. In seven municipalities a social dialog was initiated which led to establishing of Soci-economic Councils, importantly in the biggest towns in Central Serbia: Uzice, Kragujevac and Cacak.
Another great achievement was the creation of the Center for Trade Union Education, providing trainings for representatives of civil society organisations and trade unions. The Center has conducted over 100 trainings for over 2 000 union activists, workers and representatives of marginalized groups. These activities led to the adoption of a new Employment Action Plan in Uzice, as well as the stopping of the trend of reducing local budgets intended for employment financing.
The implementing partner Becej Youth Association (BYA) worked with monitoring of public spending. Their project started with monitoring of the municipal budgets first in Vojvodina and later in the whole country but after a few years, citizens inclusion in budget creation became the projects main component and contributed that currently on average some 3 500 citizens of Beej decides about budget priorities for the coming year. The communities with higher participation were the first ones to get more new investments and that was important additional motivation to continue but also and inspiration for other neighbourhoods to organise themselves better. Also two new citizens groups were formed in the process. The increased participation of women is another large positive change in Beej. Unlike in the beginning of the project when they were rarely joining the debates, today they are often even a majority in the round tables, actively advocating for their priorities. An action plan for gender equality was adopted in 2022 by the Municipality.
